summary: Curriculum Brain is an 11-agent LLM pipeline with a thin deterministic orchestrator and a git-versioned knowledge base. It turns Indian CBSE curriculum documents into a concept-skill knowledge graph with prerequisite edges (one board, three subjects, 223 released chapters), checking each chapter against a hand-written ruleset and a textbook-extracted concept map, with repair loops and human escalation. Results come from the production run history: 41.5% direct pass and 67.6% resolved without escalation over 241 runs, at $1.19 API spend per chapter. The authors state plainly that these measure internal consistency, not correctness; no item is mapped, no diagnostic model is fitted and no expert comparison is made.

claims.claim: 41.5% of 241 runs produced a Generator output passing both checks without a patch; 67.6% resolved without escalation
claims.evidence: Section 6.1 counts are internally consistent, but Check 1 uses a ruleset and Check 2 a concept map that the system itself produced; a first attempt passed both checks in 1 of 236 runs; eventual 96.4% confirmation is entailed by the loop's termination rule and the first author's sign-off.

claims.claim: After the configuration change at run 77 the rates are 57.0% and 91.5%, with escalation falling from 84.2% to 8.5%
claims.evidence: Section 6.3: nine things changed in one commit (gate rewrite, Eval and Generator models, attempt budget 3 -> 6, retry mode, prompt pruning). A matched 3-attempt cap gives 26.1%, so about a quarter of the drop is budget; a 12-chapter, 2-replicate ablation rules out the Generator model upgrade (sign test p = 0.125); the rest is unattributed. First-attempt coverage fell from 0.40 to 0.31.

claims.claim: API spend is $1.19 per chapter processed end to end
claims.evidence: Section 6.4 and Table 7 give per-agent, per-model mean cost with SD and n; the total is $216.77 across 687 run records. It excludes human review, escalation handling and engineering time, and there is no manual baseline.

claims.claim: A human rejection is encoded as a standing rule enforced on all future runs, so the system's judgment improves over time
claims.evidence: Sections 4.4 and 7: implemented but never exercised; universal_rules.md unchanged; the cross-run prompt persistence that did run leaked chapter-specific content into subject-wide prompts and was removed.

claims.claim: The released graph is a substrate for cognitive diagnosis
claims.evidence: Section 7: no CDM fitted, no student data, no item mapped; 7,448 prerequisite edges bypass verification, 99 concept pairs have edges in both directions, and generic/specific inversions were found on inspection.

patterns.note: Builds a machine-readable domain artifact (concept-skill-prerequisite graph in versioned CSVs) for downstream tools, not as context for a coding agent; no comparison with an alternative representation; 2.7% of edges are bidirectional and 5.7% of concepts isolated (Section 7).

An LLM Eval agent judges rule compliance and coverage against system-produced criteria, often with the same model that generated the output. Replacing a single LLM judgment over 31 rules with deterministic code for structural rules plus 8 LLM-judged content rules cut Check 1 failures from 77.6% to 30.7%, confounded with an Eval model change (Section 6.3).

Observational and uncontrolled: automatic write-back of the Revision agent's prompt rewrites carried chapter-specific content ('Egyptian fractions') into subject-wide prompts and grew the Mathematics base prompt to 1,544 words; it was removed and the prompt hand-pruned to 356 words (Sections 2.4, 6.3). Its effect on output quality was not measured.

Escalation to a human when the loop cannot resolve; in practice one reviewer (the first author) confirmed everything, and for genuinely failed runs an LLM coding agent wrote the resubmission feedback (Section 7). No comparison.
Eleven single-responsibility agents; the authors state there is no architectural ablation against one well-prompted call (Section 7).

methodology.sample: 241 full-pipeline runs over 168 chapters (CBSE Mathematics 1-10, Environmental Science 3-5, Science 6-10); 223 released chapters; post-hoc ablation on 12 Mathematics chapters x 2 models x 2 replicates, plus 6 chapters run through the full loop at two budgets.
methodology.baselines: None external: no manual baseline, no single-call baseline, no expert-authored Q-matrix comparison.
methodology.models: claude-sonnet-4-6, claude-sonnet-5 and gpt-5.4-mini via an OpenAI-compatible gateway; models changed mid-history.
methodology.variance: Cost SDs reported; ablation has two replicates per model and chapter with a sign test; headline rates come from one non-stationary run history.
methodology.ablations: Generator-model ablation only; no architecture, verification-gate or Eval-model ablation.

standards.artifacts: Agent code, knowledge-base template and dataset on GitHub; prompts behind successful runs recoverable only from git history

biases.detail: Pass rates measure agreement with a ruleset and a concept map produced by the pipeline itself; every confirmation was granted by the first author.
The Eval agent's judgments are never compared with experts; the same model generated and judged for most of the history.
The 96.4% eventual-confirmation figure is entailed by a loop that only terminates on confirmation or escalation and resubmits escalations (the authors say so).
The escalation drop coincides with nine simultaneous configuration changes; only the Generator model and budget are probed.
Ablation of 12 chapters with 2 replicates; a single human reviewer with no inter-rater agreement.
Per-chapter cost excludes review, escalation handling and engineering time; wall-clock time is not recorded.

coi.affiliations: AI Ready School (ed-tech company); corresponding author uses a personal address
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: The authors' own pipeline, whose output feeds the company's live curriculum visualization and an assessment-generation tool
coi.detail: A company evaluating its own system against its own criteria with no independent check. The paper repeatedly disclaims correctness and validity, which lowers the promotional risk.

verdict_reason: Off-topic for this knowledge base: it is an LLM pipeline that builds a curriculum knowledge graph, not software development with agents or the developer side of it. The evidence is internal consistency only, by the authors' own account, with a single reviewer and a confounded before/after comparison. The reporting is exemplary in its candour, and the transferable cautions are kept in applicability.
applicability: It does not inform the team's coding harness or developer onboarding. Two cautions carry over if the team adds LLM steps to healthcare-education content ingestion. First, an LLM checker that scores output against criteria the same pipeline extracted shows only internal consistency; here half the final concepts in affected chapters entered because the textbook-derived checker demanded them, so pass rates need an external reference or an expert-checked sample before they mean anything. Second, letting an agent persist its own prompt rewrites across runs leaked one chapter's specifics into subject-wide prompts. Keep rewrites run-scoped and route durable rule changes through review, which matches the team's rule that the LLM proposes and a deterministic tool commits. Moving structural checks from LLM judgment to deterministic code coincided with far fewer false failures, though that change is confounded.

conflicts_with.detail: MESH-Harness reports gains from LLM-edited harness modules selected against held-out evaluation; here, ungated cross-run persistence of LLM prompt rewrites leaked chapter-specific content and was rolled back. The difference is the evaluation gate rather than a direct contradiction.
